assessment:
In this study, Richter and colleagues investigate the neural mechanisms underlying distractor suppression in early visual cortex (EVC) using implicit statistical learning. The authors employed a variant of the additional singleton task combined with fMRI, where participants searched for orientation-defined targets while a salient color distractor appeared more frequently at one location (high-probability distractor location, HPDL). Critically, the design included omission trials where no search display was presented, allowing the authors to test whether suppression is deployed proactively. The work addresses important gaps in understanding how spatial statistical regularities shape sensory processing, specifically examining the spatial specificity, stimulus specificity, and temporal dynamics (proactive vs. reactive) of distractor suppression in EVC.

The key findings demonstrate that neural responses in EVC are significantly modulated by learned distractor probabilities. BOLD responses were suppressed at both the HPDL and nearby neutral locations compared to far neutral locations, and this suppression occurred regardless of stimulus type (distractors, targets, or neutral stimuli). Importantly, similar spatially specific suppression was observed during omission trials when no visual stimuli were presented, providing strong evidence for proactive deployment of spatial priority maps. Behaviorally, participants showed faster reaction times when distractors appeared at the HPDL (848 ms) compared to neutral locations (870-871 ms), confirming successful implicit learning. However, the neural suppression was spatially broader than the behavioral facilitation, which was specific to the HPDL. The authors provide compelling evidence against alternative explanations including explicit attentional strategies (only 35.7% correctly identified HPDL, not different from chance) and repetition suppression (randomized features, stimulus-unspecific effects, omission trial results).

The evidence supporting the main claims is solid, with appropriate statistical analyses including repeated measures ANOVAs, post-hoc tests with multiple comparison corrections, and Bayesian analyses to support null findings. The experimental design is well-controlled, using independent localizer data to define location-specific ROIs and including multiple control analyses to verify robustness across different ROI sizes and normalization approaches. The omission trial design is particularly elegant for testing proactive suppression. However, some limitations warrant consideration. The discrepancy between broad neural suppression and spatially specific behavioral effects remains somewhat speculative in its interpretation, with the authors proposing downstream refinement by higher visual areas without direct evidence. The exploratory analysis suggesting differential effects in V1 versus V2 is acknowledged as preliminary due to lack of functional retinotopy and use of volumetric rather than surface-based analysis. Additionally, the temporal resolution of BOLD fMRI cannot determine whether suppression is preceded by brief enhancement, though the authors appropriately note this would still constitute proactive suppression.

The study makes an important contribution to understanding how implicit statistical learning shapes early sensory processing through proactive, spatially broad, and stimulus-unspecific suppression. The findings advance theoretical frameworks of spatial priority maps and predictive processing in attention, demonstrating that the brain leverages learned regularities to optimize sensory processing before stimulus identification. The work will be of broad interest to researchers studying attention, statistical learning, and predictive processing, though the functional significance of the neural-behavioral dissociation and the precise mechanisms linking EVC suppression to behavioral facilitation remain open questions for future research.
